questions.title: How does the passage of time affect the validity of FOIA declarations under Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In Section II, the district court initially denied summary judgment because the Hardy declaration was 'potentially stale' due to the significant passage of time. Later, the Bender declaration was accepted as an update. I'm confused about the procedural requirement here. Does the government have a continuous burden to update declarations in FOIA litigation, or is the initial declaration sufficient unless challenged? What specific triggers the need for an updated declaration when an investigation spans several years?

questions.title: Does an ongoing criminal investigation qualify as an 'enforcement proceeding' under FOIA Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In Section IV.B, the court states that 'ongoing criminal investigations count as proceedings for these purposes,' citing CREW. I thought Exemption 7(A) required a formal proceeding like a trial, indictment, or administrative hearing. Can you clarify the doctrinal distinction between an 'investigation' and an 'enforcement proceeding' in this context? At what point does an investigation become 'reasonably anticipated' enough to trigger the exemption?

questions.title: What is the standard for 'reasonably segregable' when exempt information is interspersed throughout a document?
questions.question_body: In Section V, the court cites Mead Data Cent. to say that if non-exempt material is 'interspersed line-by-line,' it isn't reasonably segregable. I'm confused about how this applies to a massive file like Farahi's 10,750 pages. Does the 'information' vs. 'words' distinction mean agencies can withhold entire documents just because some words are exempt? Where is the line between 'inextricably intertwined' and 'reasonably segregable'?

questions.title: When is a court permitted to rely on ex parte declarations to rule on segregability in FOIA cases?
questions.question_body: In Section V, the court affirms the district court's reliance on Bender's ex parte declaration for the segregability analysis. Farahi argued this handicapped him, but the court said the problem is 'inherent' in cases where ex parte is the only way to decide without disclosure. Under what specific circumstances is the 'ex parte' process allowed to override the plaintiff's ability to challenge the withholding? Is there a limit to how much weight a court can give to sealed submissions?

questions.title: What level of deference is given to the FBI's determination that records were 'compiled for law enforcement purposes'?
questions.question_body: In Section IV.A, the court mentions the FBI is entitled to 'a fair measure of deference' but also requires a 'rational nexus' between the investigation and a law enforcement duty. How does a court balance this deference against the requirement that the agency establish a connection to a security risk or violation of law? Is the burden of proof higher for national security cases compared to standard law enforcement records?

questions.title: What constitutes 'forfeiture' of an argument on appeal in a FOIA case?
questions.question_body: In Section IV.C, the court dismisses Farahi's objection to document categories because he 'provides no specific explanation,' citing Khine v. DHS for forfeiture. Does this mean any argument not fully briefed in the initial appellate brief is waived, or is there a specific threshold for what counts as forfeiture? How does this differ from a court simply finding an argument unpersuasive?
